## Exercise 8.1: Test a switch {#ex-8.1}

The helpers `dry_run()` and `job_counts()` are already in the file, so the
test is short:

```python
def test_locus_plot_switch_removes_one_job(tmp_path):
    """make_locus_plot=False drops the locus_plot job and nothing else."""
    on = job_counts(dry_run(tmp_path))                               # <1>
    r = dry_run(tmp_path, "make_locus_plot=False")                   # <2>
    assert r.returncode == 0, r.stderr                               # <3>
    off = job_counts(r)
    assert "locus_plot" not in off
    assert off["total"] == on["total"] - 1
    assert {k: v for k, v in on.items() if k not in ("locus_plot", "total")} == \
           {k: v for k, v in off.items() if k != "total"}            # <4>
```
1. The counts with the config as it is. Comparing with this, instead of with
   61, keeps the test right when someone adds samples or turns `ttseq` off.
2. `dry_run()` puts its extra arguments after `--config outputDir=...`, so this
   becomes `--config outputDir=... make_locus_plot=False`.
3. If the dry run fails, show Snakemake's error instead of a bare "assert False".
4. Every other rule keeps its count. This is the part that catches a switch
   that removes more than it should.

With the test added, `python -m pytest tests/` reports `5 passed`.

Change `False` to `false` and the test **fails** on `"locus_plot" not in off`:
the dry run still has the plot, because `--config` passes `false` as text and
`bool("false")` is `True`. The test is doing its job. It found the same trap
module 6 showed, and that is the case for testing switches at all. A test
like this also tells you that a learner (or you, in a year) typing the
lower-case version will get the plot whether they want it or not. If that
bothers you, make `common.smk` reject anything that is not a real boolean:

```python
MAKE_LOCUS_PLOT = config.get("make_locus_plot", True)
if not isinstance(MAKE_LOCUS_PLOT, bool):                            # <1>
    raise ValueError(f"make_locus_plot must be true or false, got {MAKE_LOCUS_PLOT!r} "
                     "(on the command line, write False or True)")
```
1. YAML `true`/`false` in the config file and `True`/`False` on the command
   line are booleans; the text `"false"` is not, and now stops the run with a
   message that says how to fix it.

## Exercise 8.2: CI for RegPipe {#ex-8.2}

Start from TTpipe's workflow. Three things change: the folder, the launcher
names, and the data.

```yaml
name: RegPipe tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: course-pipeline                          # <1>
    steps:
      - name: Check out repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4                                   # <2>

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: course-pipeline/config/requirements.txt

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: |
          python -m pip install --upgrade pip
          python -m pip install -r config/requirements.txt pytest   # <3>

      - name: Check launcher scripts parse
        run: bash -n RegPipe.sh && bash -n unlock.sh

      - name: Dry-run tests
        run: python -m pytest -rs tests/                            # <4>

      - name: Fail if any test was skipped
        run: |
          python -m pytest -q tests/ | tee pytest.out
          ! grep -q skipped pytest.out                              # <5>
```
1. RegPipe lives in a subfolder of the course repository, so every `run:`
   step starts there.
2. The course data in `data/` are part of the repository (39 MB of FASTQ plus
   a few MB of reference and GEO files), so a plain checkout has them. If the
   data ever move out of git, this is where you would download them.
3. `pandas` and `pyyaml` come with `requirements.txt`. No conda: a dry run
   needs no tools.
4. `-rs` prints the reason for every skip in the log.
5. RegPipe's tests skip themselves when the data or Snakemake are missing.
   That is right on a learner's laptop and wrong in CI, where a broken
   checkout would then "pass" with zero tests run. This step makes a skip a
   failure. (It runs the tests twice; for the course data that is seconds.)

TTpipe does not need step 5, because its fixtures are in `tests/dryrun/` and
its tests do not skip on missing data.

## Exercise 8.3: Read the lint {#ex-8.3}

The linter wants f-strings instead of `+`. For `fastqc`:

```python
rule fastqc:
    input:
        fastq = fastq,
    output:
        html = f"{OUT}/{{sample}}/fastqc/{{sample}}_fastqc.html",       # <1>
        zip = f"{OUT}/{{sample}}/fastqc/{{sample}}_fastqc.zip",
    log:
        f"{LOGS}/fastqc/{{sample}}.log",
    benchmark:
        f"{BENCH}/fastqc/{{sample}}.tsv",
    threads: 1
    conda: f"{ENVS}/regpipe_align.yml"
    params:
        tmp = f"{OUT}/{{sample}}/fastqc/tmp",
```
1. In an f-string, `{OUT}` is Python's and is filled in now; `{{sample}}` comes
   out as `{sample}`, which is Snakemake's wildcard. Forgetting to double the
   braces is the usual mistake: `f"{OUT}/{sample}"` fails with
   `NameError: name 'sample' is not defined`.

The dry run still lists 61 jobs. The lint count drops from 156 to 145: all six
"absolute path" findings for `fastqc` are gone, and five of the "path
composition" ones.

Is it worth doing everywhere? The findings are style, not bugs: `OUT` comes
from the config, so nothing is hard-coded, and the paths work on any machine.
But there are two good reasons to do it anyway. Once the 156 false alarms are
gone, a new, real finding (a missing `log:`, a shell command using a global)
stands out. And the f-string form is what ChromSimPipe already uses and what
the Snakemake documentation shows, so the lab's pipelines would read the same.
Do it in one pull request per rule file, with the dry-run tests passing after
each. The field guide reaches the same conclusion for the three lab pipelines
in [What `snakemake --lint` says](../field-guide/conventions.qmd#lint).
